title: Check an unexpected reading
summary: One unexpected value can reflect a change in the crew member or a problem with the measurement. Make the two easier to tell apart.
steps: Record the original value, units, UTC time, device and any signal-quality flag.
Note activity, posture and symptoms at the time. Compare against a valid reading from the same device under similar conditions.
Use the mission’s measurement checklist for a repeat if appropriate. Keep both readings in the private crew record and share persistent or symptomatic changes with the crew medical officer.

title: Check a change in oxygen or breathing
summary: NASA identifies low oxygen and high carbon dioxide as risks during spacewalks. A wearable trend alone cannot tell whether the issue comes from the sensor, the crew member or the environment.
steps: Record oxygen and breathing readings with their timestamps and quality flags. Note whether they changed together and during what activity.
If the readings were taken in a suit or an enclosed module, check whether onboard oxygen, pressure or carbon dioxide alarms were active; use the mission’s suit or cabin procedure for any alarm.
Share breathing symptoms, the readings and environmental context with the crew medical officer. Do not alter suit or cabin settings based on a wearable.

title: Review pulse and breathing after activity
summary: Activity and the recovery interval affect the meaning of pulse and breathing trends. NASA uses exercise countermeasures to support cardiovascular and musculoskeletal function.
steps: Record the activity and when it ended. Mark which samples were taken during effort and which were taken during recovery.
Compare recovery with a prior session of similar effort when one is available. Keep symptoms and measurement quality alongside the trend.
Follow the mission exercise and medical plan if changes persist at rest or symptoms occur. Share the times and trend with the crew medical officer.

title: Document dizziness after a gravity transition
summary: NASA describes difficulty maintaining blood pressure on returning to gravity. The timing and posture help distinguish this pattern from other causes of dizziness.
steps: Record whether the dizziness started on standing, during a gravity transition, or at rest. Include when it began and any change in vision or balance.
Report symptoms to the crew medical officer. Use the mission assessment checklist rather than improvising a standing challenge.
Include available pulse and approved cuff readings with posture, time and measurement source.

title: Investigate a temperature change
summary: Skin temperature can change with exercise, suit use or the cabin environment. A wearable skin reading does not measure core temperature.
steps: Note activity, suit wear and any change in cabin conditions when the reading was taken.
Record how the crew member feels and whether the skin trend persists. If the procedure calls for body temperature, use the approved instrument.
Report environmental alarms separately through the vehicle procedure and share symptoms or persistent changes with the crew medical officer.

title: Review a blood pressure change
summary: A pressure trend is useful only when the device and measurement conditions are known. Keep wrist telemetry separate from a pressure reading taken with an approved instrument.
steps: Record both pressure values, device, posture, timing and recent activity.
For a repeat, use the mission’s approved technique and document the second value separately.
Share symptoms and comparable pressure readings with the crew medical officer rather than interpreting a single number as a diagnosis.

title: Prepare a medical handoff when Earth contact is delayed
summary: NASA requires missions to plan medical support around their operating conditions. Use the onboard plan while ground support is unavailable.
steps: Notify the assigned crew medical officer using the onboard plan.
Prepare a private update with the concern, onset in UTC, symptoms, relevant readings, actions already taken and what changed since.
Send it through the approved private medical channel when available. Keep the timeline updated while waiting.

title: Report an injury during a task
summary: The crew medical officer works within the equipment, training and procedures available on the mission. A checklist entry by itself does not establish how an injury should be treated.
steps: Notify the crew medical officer through the onboard plan and follow the mission’s injury procedure.
Report what happened, when and where, and any symptoms or changes already observed. Include relevant equipment or suit context.
Keep a short timeline for private handoff, including actions already taken under the mission procedure.

title: Check cabin air context for headache or fatigue
summary: NASA describes headache and fatigue among possible effects of elevated carbon dioxide. Those symptoms can have other causes.
steps: Note the affected location, onset, nearby activity and whether other crew members report symptoms.
Check the recorded cabin readings and any environmental alarm. Use the vehicle’s environmental response checklist if an alarm is active.
Share the environmental record and symptom timeline with the crew medical officer without inferring exposure from symptoms alone.

title: Track sleep loss and fatigue

sources.title: NASA Human Research Program: Sleep Loss Evidence Report

summary: NASA links sleep loss and changes in body-clock timing with reduced alertness and performance.
steps: Track sleep opportunity, actual sleep and interruptions against the mission schedule.
Note recent schedule shifts, noisy periods and the times when alertness dropped.
Bring recurring fatigue to the crew medical officer or operations lead before changing scheduled rest or using any countermeasure.

title: Review food and fluid intake
summary: NASA treats nutrition as a countermeasure that supports health across the mission. A short log helps reveal changes in intake amid workload or symptoms.
steps: Record meals, fluids and missed planned intake alongside activity and symptoms.
Compare logs over several days and note barriers such as limited access, workload or nausea.
Use the mission nutrition plan and share recurring changes with the crew medical officer or assigned nutrition support.

title: Log a change in vision
summary: NASA tracks vision and eye changes during long missions. Different eye problems can present similarly, and a symptom report is not enough to identify their cause.
steps: Describe what changed, when it started, and whether it affects one eye or both.
Record the task, lighting and whether the change persists. Include headache or other symptoms in the same timeline.
Notify the crew medical officer and follow the mission’s vision assessment procedure.

title: Document a radiation alert

sources.title: NASA Human Research Program: Risks of Human Spaceflight

summary: NASA identifies radiation from space as a hazard that can vary with mission location, shielding and exposure.
steps: Use the mission radiation response plan when a vehicle alarm or operations notice calls for it.
Log the alert time, location, mission activity and any available dosimeter reading.
Share the exposure record through the mission’s radiation and medical reporting channels.

title: Prepare a routine health check
summary: NASA calls for preventive monitoring of physical and psychological well-being. Consistent check-in conditions make trends easier to interpret.
steps: Follow the schedule and use the instruments in the crew health plan.
Record the value, source, time and relevant activity or symptoms. Leave a missing measure blank.
Compare with earlier checks under similar conditions and raise ongoing changes at the next appropriate medical review.
